newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Manager of Ireland's debt braces for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Manager of Ireland's debt braces for EMU.

text.p: The National Treasury Management Agency, manager of Ireland's national debt, is gearing up for European economic and monetary union despite fears that the Irish bond market could suffer if the centre of financial gravity tilts to bigger centres.
"We have a concern that we will only be one to two percent of a large market," Michael Somers, head of the NTMA told Reuters.
"We have got to ensure that we are as attractive an investment option as the larger markets and we also want to ensure that our market doesn't move offshore."
These are major concerns for the NTMA as Ireland moves enthusiastically into the first wave of states to take part in European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The agency, guardian of Ireland's 30 billion punt ($47 billion) national debt, will have to sell Irish euro bonds in competition with bigger EMU centres while preventing secondary trading from moving to more liquid markets such as London.
IRISH BOND MARKET VULNERABLE TO CENTRALISATION

A recent report by Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI), commissioned by the government, found that Ireland's bond and money markets were vulnerable to centralisation following the introduction of the euro.

"The euro is likely to create homogeneity in the money and bond markets across participating states. In the medium-term, this may lead to the emergence of one, or at most two, dominant locations within the EU where most of the trade in these assets takes place," the report said.
Somers says the Irish market has to be as competitive as possible, both structurally and in terms of the products on offer, to ensure that Irish bonds remain attractive.
The agency is seeking to eliminate a number of disadvantages in the Irish bond market such as the inability to issue STRIPS.

STRIPS, or separately traded registered interest and principal securities, are zero coupon instruments which are created as a result of trading note and bond coupons and principal repayments separately.

The NTMA says a STRIPS market is becoming a standard feature of most core European bond markets and it is currently in discussions with Ireland's finance ministry about changing the tax system to allow for their introduction in Ireland.

"We are not looking for any particular tax concessions here...what we are looking for is this to be facilitated. We have had lengthy and tortuous discussions with the Department of Finance with no success so far."
Somers says the agency is also concerned that it cannot attract private investors to the market because income is subject to the highest marginal rate of income tax.
He estimates that personal holdings in the Irish bond market are as little as five percent, low by international standards.

"It's absolutely ridiculous. You can put money with any Tom, Dick or Harry and pay 26 percent but here you have to pay 51 percent," he says. "Instead of getting money for the state we are driving it away."
NEED TO TARGET NEW INVESTORS
The NTMA, or Auntie Mae as it's known in Dublin financial circles, also believes it will have to target new types of overseas investors after EMU.
Roughly 5.5 billion punts of Irish bonds, or a third of the total, is held by overseas residents, many of whom are in the market to exploit convergence plays in the run-up to EMU.

"Clearly when convergence happens, if it happens, those people will no longer be fishing around in the market," says John Corrigan, head of domestic borrowing at the NTMA. "We have to think about a marketing strategy which will attract other investors to replace those."
One of the big new constituencies the NTMA expects to be able to tap is the life assurance business throughout Europe which is constrained by currency mismatches at the moment.
But the NTMA says it will be an uphill struggle to educate a whole new group of investors.
"We have been comfortable with a constituency of investors who have been playing spreads, playing convergence plays. We know who they are, they know the Irish economy," said Corrigan.
"They've been cultivated by ourselves and by the brokers over the years. It's not a question that life offices will walk and buy the debt. We'll have to sell the story all over again."
TOUGH TASK TO PREVENT SECONDARY TRADING OFFSHORE
Some analysts believe the agency may face an even tougher task ensuring that secondary trading in Irish bonds does not depart Dublin for London.

"While each EMU participating country will continue to make its own primary issues of bonds, where secondary trading is concerned, there is no doubt that the case for a single trading centre intensifies," Alan McQuaid of Bloxham Stockbrokers said in a recent magazine interview.
"Considering the depth and liquidity of the bond and money markets in London, it is the most obvious choice."

The introduction of market-making in late 1995 has boosted liquidity in the Irish market, attracting new investors who had previously been constrained from dealing in Irish bonds because they couldn't execute deals of an appropriate size.
The existence of the primary dealer system and the NTMA's presence as an active trader in the market may help keep secondary trading in Dublin.
Turnover on the agency's primary desk was 14.5 billion punts in 1996 while secondary trading turnover totalled 3.9 billion.

"Our intention is to continue trading," Somers says. "Because of the size of our market, we have got to be players. We are a small market ultimately and the agency has an obligation to underpin liquidity."
The need for some local knowledge to exploit differences in yields between Irish euro bonds and those of other EMU countries may also help to retain secondary trading in Dublin.
Corrigan says the spread over whatever euro bond becomes the benchmark will be determined by liquidity and Ireland's credit rating and fiscal policy at the margin.

"Monetary policy will be determined centrally so we will be looking at fiscal policy and how that measures up against the other states...We are looking at very fine-tuning on this and very fine-tuning on the spreads over whatever the benchmark euro issues are going to be," he said. ($1=.6291 Punt)
